Scented Letters: Chernobyl's Babushkas

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We get a glimpse into the daily lives of women who refused to abandon their homes after the world's most catastrophic nuclear disaster.

Unique Selling Point:
In a South African-tv first, Carte Blanche travels to the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, site of the world's worst nuclear disaster, to interview one of the area's so called self-settlers: a babushka who refused to abandon her home forever.

Summary:
This insert takes the viewer inside one of the most contaminated places on the planet. It's an area 2400 square kilometers in size, designated an exclusion zone by the Soviets in 1986 and evacuated of its residents. But, as time has gone by, some people have returned. Some a lot sooner than others. Marusha Ilchenko is one of those people. Forced to leave shortly after the accident, she and her husband returned just a year later. He has since died, but she continues to eke out an existence as one of the ever shrinking number of people who refused to leave forever.

Script:


VO: This is Maria Ilchenko. She’s 77-years-old and hasn’t been feeling well recently. Collecting water from the well adjacent to her small house in this lonely corner of northern Ukraine is more difficult than usual. But she’s putting on a brave face.

VO: I’m being driven to see her by local fixer and journalist, Dima Kolchinsky.

VO: Clearly, they’ve met before.

VO: Within minutes of our arrival, Maria is insisting we eat. She assembles a feast, including moonshine she’s made from the potatoes she grows in her small vegetable garden. In Ukraine, you don’t say no to moonshine – no matter what the hour.

VO: Later, I ask her how long she was married for.

Marusha Ilchenko Upsound in Ukanian [03:27:11]

VO: 56 years, 9 months and 9 days she says. Sadly, her husband is no longer alive.

Marusha Ilchenko [03:22:48] STRAP “Marusha “Maria” Ilchenko” He asked for my hand in 1962. On January 14th. It was the old New Year. He came to ask my hand. He got the permission, and we are in the club. There used to be the clubs back then. We gathered there as we had nothing else.

VO: It seemed a surreal conversation at times. A surreal conversation in a surreal place, on a surreal journey.

VO: It’s about 7:45 on a weekday morning and I’m about to board a train. It’s a station in a town called Slavutych, in northern Ukraine and my fellow passengers are on their way to work.

VO: It might have the appearance of an ordinary commute, but virtually all these people are heading to the same place. They’re workers at a power plant currently being decommissioned.

VO: But, not just any power plant. It’s the last of just two stops this train will make – Chernobyl.

VO: It’s 33 years ago and the Ukraine is part of what was then the Soviet Union. The reason for this emergency call is a fire in Chernobyl’s 4th reactor.

VO: What was intended as a routine safety test, ended in what remains the worst nuclear disaster in history.

ITV David Nicholls [00:15:28] Chernobyl was by far the biggest release of radiation that we've had from a single event.

VO: David Nicholls is the now retired Chief Nuclear Officer at Eskom.

ITV David Nicholls [00:01:06] STRAP “Former Chief Nuclear Officer, Eskom” And that was caused by the combination of a weak design (CUT) and the operators bypassing a series of rules and regulations because they were told they had to do the test that day.

VO: The impact on the technicians and emergency crews was graphically depicted in the HBO series, “Chernobyl”. Within weeks, 31 of them would be dead, many from radiation exposure the equivalent of 80 thousand chest x-rays in just a few hours.

ITV: David Nicholls [00:04:00] it was expected when they realized the doses they had given those early workers (CUT) they knew that a fair few of them would die.

VO: The Soviet response to the accident was to keep it under wraps. For days, those living near the reactor – people like Maria Ilchenko – were none the wiser.

ITV: Marusha Ilchenko [03:09:25] We didn't know that this thing had happened for about 3 days. Only when the people who have had their kids working on the power plant started spreading the rumor. And then I saw one of the ladies with a cow. She was working and she was crying. And I asked, “Olga, what is it? Why are you crying?" And she said, "Don't you know that there was a huge catastrophe? "

VO: And catastrophic, it was. A plume of radioactive particles billowed from the reactor and blew westwards. Conservatively, it’s estimated the disaster will eventually claim 4000 lives. Other figures are far higher.

VO: This is the abandoned town of Pripyat. At the time of the accident it accommodated the Power Plant workers and their families. 50 thousand people in all. They even had a fun fair – now, like the rest of the town, derelict and pulsing with radiation. A tailor-made, Soviet nuclear city, it was evacuated 36 hours after the accident.

Memorial: Because of its sheer scale, the evacuation of Pripyat is the one most spoken about. But, in total, 131 towns and settlements were emptied of their populations, and this rather forlorn memorial is dedicated to them.
(Shots of Chernobyl town into shots from the bridge)

VO: One of those was Chernobyl town. 15 km from the power plant, it was once home to 14000 people. It was evacuated nine days after the accident but, more than 30 years on, it’s very unlike Pripyat.

Chernobyl town: You wouldn’t describe Chernobyl town as a hive of activity but there are a surprising number of people living and working here – going about their daily lives as they would anywhere else in the world. And yet it’s still a little surreal because here, humans appear out of place.

VO: But here they are: bakers making their early deliveries; shopkeepers taking care of the morning trade, technicians and clerks on their way to work.

VO: Shortly after the accident, a 30km exclusion zone was declared around the power plant. The area is still considered one of the most contaminated in the world but, in places – like Chernobyl town – background radiation levels are no higher than you’d expect in Jo’burg or Cape Town. So, it shouldn’t be too surprising that some have come back.


VO: Maria is one of those who returned to the Exclusion Zone, but her homecoming was more complex. Like the hundred and 20 thousand other people evacuated in 1986, she and her husband were told they’d return to their home, about 20 drive minutes south of the plant, within days.

ITV Marusha Ilchenko [03:11:15] [They said] “Take food for 3 days. Take the money you need and your passports.” My late husband took an axe. Two cups, two plates. For three days. It was Easter. So we took an Easter cake, bacon. I baked the Easter cake. Eggs. And we moved away. Left all we had there.

VO: Days became weeks, and weeks became months. They were settled on a collective farm – the authorities no longer keeping up the pretense that they’d be sent home. Maria’s husband made it home briefly, sent on a morbid mission. She went back, too, although… illegally.

ITV Marusha Ilchenko [03:13:17]: My husband was sent there to bury chickens, dogs and cats. And I crawled under the wire fence illegally in order to look after the potatoes. The police took me out.

VO: The indignity of sneaking back only came to an end more than a year after first being evacuated. She and her husband joined more than a hundred others in returning to their homes in the Exclusion Zone. At the time Maria’s son was in the army. She broke the news to him in a letter.

ITV Marusha Ilchenko [03:15:57]: He wrote back: "Mom, even if it is a land of milk and honey, do not stay in Gruzske, go home. And I will come there. And may my father will drive the tractor. And we will be sitting under grandma’s willow.” And we went home.

VO: As we’re talking, it’s hard to reconcile Maria’s vivid memories of that time with what Chernobyl has slowly become.

VO: The infamous reactor 4 is now covered by a state-of-the-art containment structure, which was rolled into place in 2016. With the worst of its radioactive material contained, it’s now become a selfie hotspot. Along with several others in the Zone.

Radiation: One of the questions we get asked – and indeed one that we ask ourselves – is how high the radiation levels are here. And it’s actually quite a difficult question to answer because the levels vary depending on where in the exclusion zone you are. Here, the levels are relatively high but, as you can see, it’s not deterring the tourists.

VO: And, if you stay on the designated paths, relatively high is still within safe limits – no more they say than the dose you receive from cosmic radiation on a six-hour flight. And while some experts dispute that, thousands of tourists are still drawn here. As was Maria, and more than a hundred other so called self-settlers, all those years ago.

ITV Marusha Ilchenko [03:19:09]: So many people came to me here to measure radiation. And here in the corner was put something like a globe, like a big sphere. And some man said to my husband, "Grandpa, cut the tree and take it away. And also get rid of the bench near the small window. We have found nothing harmful here."

ITV David Nicholl [00:15:28] there was no question that evacuating the immediate area around Chernobyl was an appropriate measure (CUT) How long for is the key question? When do you go back? How much do you clean up? (CUT) And if you say you want to get it absolutely clean, it's almost impossible to get there.
Self-settlers 2: If you’re able to ignore the catastrophic nuclear disaster 33 years ago, this life actually might have its attractions. They were certainly powerful enough to draw Maria back here in 1987. Is she happy? Well, the impression I have is that it’s all relative. The people here are simply doing the best they can with what they have.

VO: Although I wondered whether the surge in tourism to Chernobyl might in some way shape their future – perhaps for the worst.

ITV Dima Kolchinsky [00:06:11] STRAP “Ukrainian Producer” I don't think there is anything that that would be able to spoil them because after all it said it's a sort of a kind of in a way heroic act to come back to the place like that. And as long as they are in the way, those everyday heroes it's really hard to break a person like that.

JOHN QUESTION: How important is it for tourists to have the right attitude?

ITV Dima Kolchinsky [00:05:16] there is no need to kind of to meditate on the issue before you come here (CUT) The mood will come over here or it won't come over here and if it's not coming over then this person is basically unconscious, you know? It's an infantile person who you know who doesn't learn the lesson.

VO: In other words, how you experience Chernobyl shouldn’t be prescribed. Its lessons are in plain view to those prepared to see them.

“Every lie we tell incurs a debt to the truth. Sooner or later that debt is paid.”

VO: That quote featured in the final episode of HBO’s Chernobyl series – attributed to one of the officials who helped reveal the truth about the accident. I thought about it a lot during my time in Ukraine, and I wondered whether Chernobyl had fully repaid its debt. To the families of those who died, the people who fell ill. And to people like Maria.

VO: I asked her if she’s still happy she came back all those years ago. “If I hadn’t”, she replied, “I would have been long dead.” (ENDS)

metadata.Unique Selling Point: In a South African-tv first, Carte Blanche travels to the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, site of the world's worst nuclear disaster, to interview one of the area's so called self-settlers: a babushka who refused to abandon her home forever.
metadata.Summary: This insert takes the viewer inside one of the most contaminated places on the planet. It's an area 2400 square kilometers in size, designated an exclusion zone by the Soviets in 1986 and evacuated of its residents. But, as time has gone by, some people have returned. Some a lot sooner than others. Marusha Ilchenko is one of those people. Forced to leave shortly after the accident, she and her husband returned just a year later. He has since died, but she continues to eke out an existence as one of the ever shrinking number of people who refused to leave forever.
